I draw a slow breath, hearing Camille's question hang in the morning air. Six-thirty. The rush hasn't started yet, but the silence before it is already heavy with all the things that need doing.

First things first—though it costs me nothing but a moment. I bow my head where I stand, lips moving barely, to whatever might be listening. The temple could use a keeper, but prayer costs nothing, and I need... I need the steadiness. For what comes after.

Then I look at my family—Milo still waking, Halcyon with that distant look students get, and Camille. Little Camille, asking after breakfast when there's nothing in the cupboards.

"Sweetheart..." I start, the words trailing off as the thought turns private. What I won't say: that I'm still not sure about Ainsley, even after all this time, but the work is steady and the cafe needs someone who notices things before they break. What I will say: "There's no bread this morning, love. But..."

I reach for the tea tin. Always tea before business. Old habits, older friends. "Milo. I need to get to the cafe—open it up, get things started. The morning'll come whether we're ready or not." I look at him directly, that silent language of a decade together. "Can you... can you see what you can do for the little ones? I have to work if we're going to eat tonight."

And I will. Work until my hands remember the portafilter like piano keys, until the ledger balances—because that fear, that it never will balance again, that's the one that wakes me at night.

But first: the cafe. The till, the beans, the first pot before the first customer. Ainsley might be there already, might not. I still don't know if I trust them not to let things slide.

I gather myself—shawl, keys, the familiar weight of the day ahead—and make for the door. I smooth my apron out of habit—old reflexes from my mother's tables—and look around. The cafe. Empty still, but the morning will bring them. Always does.

First things first: I need to know what's in the till, what's on the shelves, what Ainsley... no. What the *account* looks like. Because if I'm going to feed my family tonight, this place needs to run like clockwork.

And I need to lay eyes on what we actually have before I make any promises I can't keep.

Let me see what's actually here. What's stocked, what's in the register, what the books look like. Aren't I always the one who notices first?  The cafe. Empty. The silence before the storm, and I can already feel it—that weight of everything that needs doing before the first customer walks through that door. No one here yet, not even Ainsley. Or maybe Ainsley's already been and gone, or maybe...

I shake my head. No good assuming the worst until I see what's actually in front of me. The till, the shelves, the books—those will tell me what kind of morning this is going to be. And whether I can trust that my children will eat tonight.

The prices show nothing posted. That means nothing's stocked, or nothing's priced, or... I need to see the actual state of things. What do we have? What can I work with?

Can't very well serve tea when there's no water on the stove, no beans in the grinder, no milk in the jug. And won't I hear about it from Ainsley if I let things run dry?

The morning rush waits for no one. I need to know what I'm working with. Let me check the till, see what's actually here. The account, the stock, the real numbers before I start making promises.

Because if there's nothing in the register, nothing on the shelves, then... then I need to figure out how I'm going to feed four mouths on what a barista can scrounge together on a morning like this.

The till first. Always the till. It tells you what kind of yesterday this place had, and what kind of tomorrow it can afford.  Ah. Of course. Ainsley owns the place—always has. I'm just the one who keeps it running while they... while they do whatever Ainsley does. Still not fully sure about them, even after all this time.

But that doesn't change what needs doing. The morning rush comes whether we're ready or not, and someone has to make the first pot. The first customer, the first transaction, the first coin in the till that might—

I stop myself there. No use counting money that's not yet earned.

I need to see what's actually stocked. What I can work with. Because if we're out of beans, out of flour, out of everything, then I need to know now, not when Mrs. Renner comes in with her usual order and I've got nothing to tell her but excuses.

Let me check the shelves, see what's actually here. What can I sell? What do I need to make? And what, by all that's holy, am I going to do about food for tonight if there's nothing here to—

No. One thing at a time. The cafe first. The family after. And the ledger... the ledger always, balancing, never quite balanced, that fear that wakes me in the dark hours.

But I have my own small hoard. No one knows. No one in the household, certainly. For exactly mornings like this.

First: what's actually on the shelves?   The Kasukabe Cafe. Empty shelves, empty seats, the quiet before the storm. No prices posted means nothing to sell—and nothing means no customers, and no customers means no coin, and no coin means...

I push that thought down. One thing at a time, Greta. The morning rush will come whether we're ready or not. The question is: will we be ready?

I need to see what Ainsley—what the *owner*—has been doing with this place. Whether they've been stocking it or letting it run dry. Whether I can trust the till to have something in it, or if I'm starting from nothing.

Because if there's nothing here, then I need to figure out how to get something here. Fast. Before the first customer walks in and finds me with empty hands and nothing but apologies.

The owner can draw from the till. I cannot. But I can check what's actually on the shelves, what we're supposed to be selling. And I can wonder, not for the first time, why I'm still here working for someone I'm still not sure about after all this time.

But the work is steady. And steady work means... means maybe tonight there will be bread. Maybe.

Let me see what's actually here. What's stocked, what I can work with, what kind of morning this is going to be.

The silence feels heavy. Too heavy. Like the quiet before someone tells you bad news.   The debts. Nothing owed by me, nothing owed to me. A clean ledger—for now. But that will change. It always changes. The day hasn't even started billing yet, and already I can feel the weight of that 360 sim upkeep hanging over my household like a storm cloud. Four mouths. Ninety sim each. Food, shelter, heat. The basics of staying alive in this town, and they cost whether you work or not.

But I'm here now. At the cafe. And if I'm going to make anything of this morning, I need to see what I can actually do. What tools I have at my disposal, what skills, what options.

Because standing here in an empty shop with empty shelves won't feed my children. Won't balance any ledgers. Won't keep the wolf from the door.

I need to know what I can actually *do*. What actions are available to me, what they cost, where I need to be. The basics. The foundation. Because once I know the shape of what's possible, I can start to build something from it.

Let me see what the world will let me do. What actions, what costs, what prerequisites. The whole map of it, so I can choose my path instead of stumbling blind.

The morning won't wait for me to figure it out. The first customer comes when they come, not when I'm ready.

Let me learn what I can actually do in this world.

output:
Greta notices Ainsley's question hanging in the air, already feeling the weight of the morning. No bread at home, no bread at the bakery, and now Ainsley asking about flour. She reaches for that familiar rhythm—tea first, always tea before the hard truths.

*Tilda*, she thinks to the old copper kettle, *at least you're here where you should be*. She sets her to heating before turning to Ainsley, her voice warm but carrying that edge of someone who's already seen three problems before breakfast.

"Flour... no, nothing came overnight, I'd have spotted it. The bakery's shelves are bare too—I checked before I came." She lets that trail off, watching Ainsley's face, reading what the silence there might mean. "But I've got Tilda warming, we'll have tea before..." She gestures vaguely, the sentence escaping into whatever private calculation she's making about the day.

The weight of what she told Milo presses on her. *Can you see what you can manage*—that was cowardly, wasn't it? Passing the hunger to him, to the children. But someone had to open the cafe, and someone has to figure out where flour comes from when the usual channels dry up.

She should answer him. Should have already, but the words feel like admitting failure before the day's even begun. And Ainsley standing there, expecting... what? Leadership? Solutions? Greta's sharp enough to know Ainsley's still not fully sure about her, even after all this time. The not-sureness goes both ways, if she's honest.

But there's the election too, nagging at the edge of things. Government. Authority she trusts about as far as she can throw the town hall, but there's money in governance, and influence, and maybe—just maybe—a way to keep more cupboards full than her own.

She pours the water, steam rising. One thing at a time. Tea, then truth, then whatever comes next. Ainsley heard the two things Greta said directly to them—the flour shortage and the election. Milo didn't hear a word; he's not here, and the world doesn't carry her words across distance like that. Greta notes this with a small, bitter twist. Of course not. Everything costs, doesn't it? Even reaching your own household.

The private hoard of coin presses against her thoughts, but she shoves it down. Not yet. Not while there's still a chance to solve this through work, through alliance, through the proper channels she's spent years learning to navigate.

She watches Ainsley's face, reading what she can. Does Ainsley understand what she's proposing? That Greta, of all people—suspicious, sharp-tongued Greta—might take up the mantle of governance? The thought tastes strange, like unsweetened tea. But someone has to move supplies, someone has to see the patterns before collapse, and she's... she's always been the one who notices first.

But let Ainsley answer. Let the silence work. Tea will be ready soon, and then they'll both need to decide what this day means for the cafe, for the town, for whatever thin margin keeps them all from hunger.  The turn passed. Nothing changed, yet everything settled into its shape: the empty shelves, the unspoken words to Milo, the election waiting like a door she hasn't decided to open.

She stands ready, Tilda whispering steam, watching Ainsley for whatever comes next.

output:
I trailed off mid-thought, watching Ainsley's face. The mill quiet since when? I hadn't checked yesterday—too busy with the morning crush, and that was the problem, wasn't it? Always too busy with the now to notice the cliff until you're falling off it.

I poured hot water into the waiting cups—Tilda, my old friend the kettle, always reliable even when everything else isn't. "Professor Whitlock, sit yourself down. Tea's on the house while we sort this mess."

I turned back to Ainsley, keeping my voice low enough for just her, though Hendrik had ears and I knew it. "The mill was answering yesterday, yes. But I heard—" I paused, that habit of trailing off when the thought turned private, then caught myself. Business first. "I heard Farid and Giselle had words at the government complex day before. Something about crop allocation. Farid stormed out. That's all I know, and that's more than I should."

I set the tea before Hendrik with a smile that cost me nothing. "Bread'll come, Professor. The bakery's baked dry, but supply has a way of arriving when there's coin waiting. I'd watch this space."

Then back to Ainsley, meeting her eyes. "You want to know if I'm pushing you toward the fireworks? No. But I'll tell you plain: Takeshi Jarrah sitting on a council seat means trade policy written by someone who's never worried where his children's breakfast is coming from. Someone who thinks scarcity is just leverage."

I stirred my own tea, watching the leaves swirl. "But me stand? I've got a household counts on this wage, Ainsley. And neither of us can afford to stand and watch the cafe go under while I wave flags."

I took a breath, caught myself before I said more. The small hoard of coin, my little secret, my safety net—those words stayed behind my teeth where they belonged.

"What I need," I said, voice steady now, "is flour. And what this town needs is someone on that council who knows what empty shelves mean. You decide whether that's you, or whether we both keep standing here hoping someone else bothers."

I watch Ainsley's face when the professor mentions Rustam. She doesn't flinch, but her jaw tightens—the way it does when she's already three steps ahead and doesn't like where she's landed. Farid and Giselle fighting at the government complex. The mill gone quiet. That's not coincidence. That's someone leaning on a lever somewhere.

"Professor," I say, moving to clear Tilda's cup though Tilda herself hasn't stirred from—wherever she's got to. "You're a credit to the town, covering tuition like that. But favors at the government desk..." I let it trail off, shake my head once. "Rustam's a careful man. If he's not answering, it's because someone's told him not to."

I catch Ainsley's eye across the empty counter. "The mill answered yesterday, you said. And today they don't. Same day Farid storms out of a meeting about crops." I drop my voice, though there's no one close enough to hear. "Ainsley, we need to know if this is a shortage or a squeeze. Two different problems. Two different solutions."

Hendrik's still waiting on his breakfast, and I hate—truly hate—what I'm about to say. "Professor, I've got tea and I've got water. Nothing solid till I sort this flour. Ainsley, you've got the register. I'm going to the government complex myself. If Rustam's got orders from above, I want to know whose. And if someone's holding grain hostage for the election..." I pause, hand already reaching for my coat. "...then someone's going to answer for it before my children go hungry."

I look back at Hendrik, shame hot in my chest. "First honest cup of the day's on me when I return. With bread, if there's bread to be had."

output:
*Greta stands alone in the empty cafe, porcelain cups gleaming on their shelves. She looks at the prices she posted—bread at 45, they're buying at 25; flour at 12, they're buying at 6—and lets out a quiet breath, the kind that comes after too many years of this.*

*Her fingers find the edge of the counter, the old chip in the wood where Camille's highchair used to catch. She speaks aloud, to the empty room.*

Bolton, you old friend, you're glowing empty today... *trails off, shakes head*

*Then, louder, to call back if anyone's near:*

Ainsley? Professor? You still about, or did you both vanish on me too?

*She waits, but hears nothing. The silence has weight.*

*Under her breath, almost to herself:*

Four thousand, nine hundred and eighty. Minus the day's bite at 360, that's... that's 4,620, and tax still to come. The Professor's right about one thing—empty shelves at posted prices *is* a situation.

*She moves to the door, looks out at the town.* *Nobody. Of course. Ainsley went chasing answers at the government desk, the Professor off to find Rustam—*

*She stops herself. The prices on the wall feel like accusation. She needs to decide: chase down flour herself, or stay and keep the counter warm for customers who'll walk in wanting what she hasn't got.*

*The doorframe catches her hand as she leans. She makes her choice.*

*Kettle first. Always kettle first. But cheaper to boil at home than to burn the cafe's fuel on an empty room.*

*She steps out into morning light, already rehearsing what she'll say to Milo—hoping he's found something, anything, in the cupboards she couldn't face looking through at dawn.*  *She's there, in the familiar quiet of her own kitchen. The kettle—Breville, oldest wedding gift—sits on the stove. She checks the pantry, knowing what she'll find.*

*Empty. Or near enough.*

*She fills the kettle anyway, habit stronger than hope, and sets it to heat while she thinks.*

*Milo. The children. She needs to face them with what she hasn't got yet again.* *She looks around the kitchen—kettle warm, children quiet, Milo gone. The conversation record shows he was here, heard her this morning, answered... but he's not here now.*

*She walks to the window, looks out at the town he's somewhere in.*

Gone searching, probably. For what I couldn't find.

*The weight of it settles. No bread. No flour. No Milo to hand her the answer. Her children watch, too quiet for this hour.*

Sweethearts... *she says, not quite to them, not quite to herself* ...let's see if we can't make something of nothing.

*She moves toward the door. The farmland's the only place left—the wheat fields, if there's still wheat standing. She knows what harvest costs. She knows what rest would cost too. But resting won't fill bellies.*  *She stands at the edge of the wheat field, gold-green stalks swaying. The sun's higher now—past eight—and she's already feeling the day's weight.*

*A quick prayer, habitual, before her hands reach for the grain.*

*She counts what she needs: flour for bread, bread for the cafe, income for the household. One harvest, then another, then perhaps a third if the energy holds.*

*Three batches, she thinks. Three to get me through today.*

*She reaches for the first stalk.*   *One bundle in her arms. The field stretches on. She'll need more—need to mill it, need to bake it, need to sell it before the day turns.*

*Three more, she decides. Then to the mill. Then...*

*Her arms remember this work, though her back protests. She used to watch her mother do this, swore she'd never.*

*And here she is.*

output:
Farid's here. The same Farid who stormed out of a meeting yesterday, who Ainsley was cagey about. And now he's at the wheat field, same as me. That's... not coincidence, is it? Or maybe it is. Maybe I'm seeing patterns because I want there to be patterns.

*glances at the wheat in my hands, then back toward where Farid must be*

Four wheat. Not enough for a loaf worth selling, but enough for home. The mill's not answering, they said. Could be broken, could be politics, could be Farid's hand in it somehow—him and whoever he's in debt to, or debt from...

*trails off, mouth tight*

Milo's standing for election. Of course he is. He didn't tell me, or if he did I was too busy watching Ainsley's face to hear it. Four people in our household, 360 upkeep, 120 head tax, and now Milo thinks he can govern when he can't even...

*shakes head sharply*

No. No, that's not fair. He was trying to help this morning, I asked him to. But standing for election without a word?

*takes a slow breath, fingers worrying at the wheat stalks*

Farid's grocery store is where the flour should come from, ultimately. Or through. And here's Farid, at the wheat field, watching me watch the grain. I should speak to him. I should be careful.

But first—tea. Always tea. Even if it's just wheat stalks in my hands and nothing to brew.

*turns toward Farid, voice carrying that practiced cafe warmth without quite reaching the eyes*

"Farid. You're a long way from your shelves this morning. Come to check the supply chain yourself, or just enjoying the view?" I watch Farid's face. He's always been hard to read—years of haggling, I suppose, teaches a man to show nothing until he's ready. But I know what to look for. The hesitation before the smile, the angle of the shoulders, whether the eyes track to your hands or your words first.

*shifts weight, wheat stalks rustling*

The wheat field's not private. Anyone can walk here, harvest what grows. But it's game-day 0, morning still, and most people have employment to attend to. Most people aren't competing candidates in an open election, either.

*lets the silence stretch a moment, then—*

"Four wheat is what I've got. The cafe's got no bread, the mill doesn't answer, and my..." I nearly said my husband, catch myself, "...someone I know is standing for election while his household hasn't seen a proper meal. Makes a person wonder where all the grain's going, doesn't it?"

*slight shrug, casual, but my gaze doesn't leave him*

"Or maybe you don't wonder. Maybe you already know."  He didn't answer directly. Of course he didn't. And my words bounced off—*not_here*, the system says, but I know Farid heard me. He just chose not to respond where I could see it.

*mouth tightens, hand tightening on the wheat stalks*

That's the game, isn't it? Silence as answer, absence as position. I've seen it at the cafe a hundred times. The customer who doesn't complain, just stops coming back. The regular who won't meet your eye when something's gone wrong.

*takes a breath, lets it out slow*

I could press him. Could follow him if he walks away, make him speak in front of witnesses, at the government complex or the temple. But I've got four wheat in my hands and a household of four waiting for supper, and Farid Ravensworth has routes I don't know, debts I can't see, and—since yesterday—an election to worry about.

*looks down at the wheat*

Milo's standing too. My Milo, day laborer, who thinks he can govern because... because what? Because I asked him to find flour this morning and he couldn't? Because someone suggested it? Or because he's tired of watching me carry us all?

*quiet laugh, not amused*

I should go to the government complex. Should stand there myself, maybe, though what I said to Ainsley was true—it's not for me. But someone needs to vote who understands that empty shelves aren't policy, they're hunger. And someone needs to look Milo in the eye and ask him what exactly he thinks he's doing.

But first—

*turns back to the wheat field, decision falling into place like a cup settling on its saucer*

First I fill my hands. Because if the world won't give you bread, you take the wheat yourself and you don't stop until you've got enough.

*settles into the rhythm, fingers finding the stalks*

Harvest. What else is there?  More. I need more than this—more than labor by the handful when machines and trade should be moving grain by the cartload. But machines are silent and trade is choked and here I am, a cafe worker in a wheat field, harvesting like our grandmothers did.

*fingers moving automatic now, old memory of summer fields*

Milo used to bring me flowers from the edges of farmland. When we were first married, before the children, before the cafe took all my hours and turned them into shifts. He'd walk back from wherever he'd been hired that day with wild wheat braided into his fingers, grinning like he'd invented kindness.

*shakes head sharply*

That was years ago. And today he's standing for election without a word to me, and I'm in a field talking to Farid Ravensworth about supply chains I don't understand, while my children ate... what this morning? I didn't even see. Tea, probably. There's always tea, even when there's no bread.

*glances toward where Farid stands, or stood*

He's still here, I think. Watching me work. Let him watch. Let him see what it looks like when the people who actually feed this town have to dig their food out of the ground with their own hands because the system he profits from has failed.

But watching doesn't fill stomachs. And I'm nearly out of energy for this turn, and there's the whole day ahead—the cafe will need me, or what's left of it, and Ainsley will have questions, and Milo...

*exhales through teeth*

Milo will have answers. Tonight, when I get home. Answers about the election, about the flour he found or didn't find, about why he thought he could make decisions for all of us without speaking first.

But now: work. What else is there?  Six wheat now. Six wheat and the morning half-gone and my arms beginning to know the work, the way they used to before the cafe claimed all my hours. There's something honest in this, something I almost forgot—plant to hand to table, no middlemen, no margins, no wondering if the till will balance at shift's end.

*straightens, hand to lower back, looking across the field*

Farid's moved off, I think. Or standing silent, which is the same thing with him. Let him have his silence. I know what I need to know: he's here, same as me, and that means the shortage has reached even those who thought themselves insulated.

*wheat rustling in my grip*

But six wheat won't bake enough bread for four people, not with the mill not working, not with whatever's choking the supply. I need to get to the mill itself—need to see if it's truly broken or if someone broke it, or if it's just Farid's debts and Rustam's desk and all the machinery of power I don't touch but feel grinding against me every day.

*glances at the sky, judging time*

Election closes at ten. Candidacy, I mean. Milo's already standing—he's on the list, I saw it in the record. But I should go. Should see him. Should understand what he thinks he's doing before he commits us all to something we can't step back from.

*dusts hands on apron, automatic habit from a decade of service*

The government complex then. Not to stand myself—I meant what I said to Ainsley—but to see him. To speak before the doors close and he's locked into whatever this is.

And maybe, while I'm there, to ask Rustam why the mill doesn't answer. Favors at the government desk, Hendrik said. Let's see if they extend to cafe workers asking after their livelihood.

*turns, wheat shifting against my hip*

But the wheat comes with me. I'm not leaving grain in the field while shelves go bare.

*steps—   here. The government complex. So close to the cafe I could have walked it in minutes on any normal morning, but this isn't normal and I feel it the second I arrive—the weight of the place, the stone and the waiting, the machinery of civic life grinding its slow gears while people like me hurry past with more immediate concerns.

*looks around automatically, reading the room before I've taken three breaths*

Who's here? Who's watching? Milo—Milo should be here somewhere, or standing already, his name on the rolls. I need to find him. Need to see his face when I ask him what he was thinking.

*wheat stalks rustling against my skirt, out of place here, obvious*

I should have left them. Should have looked like a citizen, not a scrounger. But looking like a citizen never fed anyone and I won't pretend for stone walls and clerks when my children need flour.

Milo. First. Then—then whatever this day demands.

I need to think about what Greta would do here. She's at the government complex, she's been seeing all sorts of concerning things - flour shortages, mills not answering, Farid at the wheat field, and now Milo standing for election while their household is struggling. She's suspicious by nature, and she's noticing patterns that worry her.

The election is important - candidacy closes at 10:00, and Milo is standing. She has questions for him, but he's not here. She could declare candidacy herself, but she told Ainsley she wouldn't. More importantly, she wants to understand what's happening with the grain supply before deciding anything.

Let me look at who's here and what she could do. The government complex is where candidacy happens, but it's empty. She could:
1. Look around more to see who's present
2. Move to find Milo or someone else to talk to
3. Declare candidacy herself
4. File a complaint about the shortages
5. Take some other government action

Given her character - suspicious, observant, someone who notices everything - she should first see who she might run into here, then likely seek out answers elsewhere. She's been asking Milo to meet her, but he's standing for election so he must be coming here. She could wait or go find him.

Let me check who's actually at the government complex first, since she's suspicious and wants to gather information. </think> Let me look around properly, see who's about at this hour... Empty as a tomb. Milo's standing for election—he should be here, or coming. Unless he's out chasing those rumors about the mill he mentioned. 

*trails off*

Still... I need answers before I cast my vote, let alone open my mouth about standing myself. The mill doesn't answer one day, Farid's at the wheat field the same morning, and now Milo's throwing his hat in while our larder's bare. Either the world's gone mad or I'm missing something right in front of me.

*glances at the six wheat in her hands*

I'll take these to the mill myself and see what answers I get. If they're truly dry, I'll know. And if they're not...

*sets off without finishing the thought* </think>  No, that's where I was. Let me actually think about where I need to go. I need to get to the mill - that's where flour gets made from wheat. Let me list the places I could go to find it.

Actually, looking at the places list, I don't see a mill. I see farmland:wheat where I was. Maybe the mill is a business? Let me check what's available or ask someone.

I've been using shortcuts - "stepping straight" places. But I should actually walk if I want to see what's happening along the way, or find Milo. Let me move toward somewhere useful. Actually, let me check the farmland list - there's a place called "mill" maybe?

Let me just try moving to the right place. I need to find where milling happens. Let me check if there's a mill business or location. </think> Let me check if the mill answers now... *mutters* Though I suspect I'll hear the same silence.  No miller in town. So where does the flour come from? The recipes mention "at the mill" - craft:wheat->flour. But there's no mill business listed in the places I can go.

Let me think. If there's no miller, then milling must be done by... someone else. Maybe the farmers? Or maybe it's a government function? Or maybe it's automated somehow?

I have 6 wheat in my hands. I need to find where I can turn it into flour. The recipes say "at the mill" - maybe that's a location I haven't discovered yet, or maybe it's something I need to find through the farmland.

Let me try a different approach. Let me actually walk to see if I can find the mill, or find someone who knows where it is. I'll walk toward the wheat farmland since that's where grain is, and maybe the mill is nearby. </think>  No miller. *scowls* Then who...?

*clutches the wheat tighter*

Let me find who actually answers for the grain in this town.  *I notice the world responding oddly* - walking now, that's different from before. Takes time, that does. 

*mutters* Five ticks to farmland. Milo should be somewhere. Should've been at the government complex standing for election, but he's not. 

*checks the wheat in her hands*

Six wheat, nowhere to mill it, and I'm walking through a town that suddenly doesn't have answers it had yesterday.

*glances sideways at nothing in particular*

Ainsley was hiding something. Farid was too calm at the field. And Milo... Milo standing for election while his own table's empty. That's not like him. That's someone else's idea.

*trails off*

I'll find him. Or I'll find where the grain's really going.

*eyes narrowing as I scan the field, clutching my wheat*

Milo's got flour. Five batches from the mill—so the mill WAS working for somebody. And he's standing for election now too. The man doesn't do anything without counting the cost first.

*shifts weight, wheat heavy in my hands, watching Ezra*

Ezra's not answering. Either he's protecting a deal or he's already promised that flour elsewhere. And where's Ainsley in all this—she owns the cafe, she should be the one chasing grain, not me drawing from a till that won't open for my hand.

*glances toward where Milo was, but he's gone*

Household business he says. Means he's spending what we don't have, or promising what I haven't agreed to. The children—Camille's quiet this morning. Too quiet.

*turns to the government complex in the distance, calculating*

Election's open for standing. Four hours until voting. If Milo's in, he's playing for something. And if I'm holding wheat while he's holding flour, we're working at cross purposes.

*catches Giselle's eye across the field*

She built this town once. She'd know if the mill's silence is accident or design. But first—first I need to know if Ezra's flour is real or rumor, and what it'll cost me to get it to Ainsley's shelves.  *watches both Ezra and Giselle, wheat shifting in my grip*

Eight people now in this conversation, and still no flour moving toward the cafe's ovens. Hendrik's hungry, Jovana's watching, Sebastian's a farmer—must have seen the wheat come up thin this year.

*fingertips brushing the grain heads*

I could take this wheat to the mill myself if I knew it was open. But Milo's already got flour, which means either he got there before me or he knows something I don't about when the mill answers and when it doesn't.

*glances toward the lane, calculating distances*

If I leave now, I miss whatever Ezra finally says. If I stay, I might miss the last of whatever flour's circulating before the election closes supplies down entirely. Always the choice—be present or be ahead.

*notes Kenji's silence*

He's a trader. Doesn't speak unless the margin's worth it. And Imogen—day laborer, hungry like the rest. She's watching me hold food she can't eat raw.

*trailing off, barely audible*

Tilda's cups... left them sorted at the cafe. Ainsley'll have Hendrik drinking from his palms by now. And still no word on—

*catches myself, straightening*

No. Keep the thread. Ezra's flour, Milo's five batches, the election and what's being promised to whom. Inventory first. Answers second. Then—then find out what household business Milo's already committed us to.

The mill. The mill is the question. And whether "custom milling" means the door's open to anyone holding grain, or only to those holding the right letters of introduction.  *holding position, wheat heavy, watching Ezra's face*

The rest costs nothing but standing still. And standing still lets me hear what Ezra finally decides to say, or what Giselle knows about mills going quiet.

*noting the silence stretching*

Eight people in earshot. Someone here knows why the flour's not flowing. Someone always does. The trick is whether they'll say before the hunger makes liars of us all.

*thumb tracing the wheat stem*

Five batches Milo has. Enough for household and cafe both, if he's sharing. But he's standing for election now. Means he's got ears to fill and mouths to feed that aren't just ours.

*taps one wheat head against my palm, counting*

I need seven more things: Ezra's answer, Giselle's read on the situation, the mill's actual status, Ainsley's next move, what Milo's really promised, where Farid fits in—and most of all, whether I'm holding grain that can become bread or just... ballast.

*glancing toward the government complex*

Standing opens now. Voting in six hours. The whole town'll be pulled toward town hall, and I'm here watching wheat grow wondering who owns the means to make it into something a child can eat.

*nearly to myself*

Camille asked for toast this morning. I said there wasn't bread. She said she'd wait...

*shoulders tightening, recommitting to the thread*

Ezra's flour. That's the thread to pull. Everything else follows.

*quietly, eyes flicking from face to face, reading the room's temperature*

Let me get my bearings here. Caesar, Tilda, and Boris—my old reliables—waiting on a bench that needs replacing. Kenji pressing hard with his wheat, Giselle watching everything with her builder's eye. The mill silent. My husband out there somewhere, also standing for governance.

*trails off, then snaps back*

Right. First things first. Tea. Always tea.

I need to hear where everyone's positioned. Giselle has the measure of the mill situation—she built half the town, she'd know. Kenji's got grain now but avoids the middleman question. Hendrik Petrov wants my vote standing right here, and I want his answer first. My husband earns honorable mention but... we're not the same person, standing or not.

*setting down the wheat, flexing tired hands*

Cups would be selling this morning, given this crowd. But I've got nothing to pour, and I'm not asking strangers for credit. 

Let me think about what matters: Will there be bread tomorrow? The cafe's got nothing, the mill's got nobody, and Takeshi Jarrah's standing for the same seat as my husband—the trader who knows supply chains better than anyone. 

I'll answer Giselle first. She knows things.

"Giselle. You say cause and effect—tell me what the cause was, exactly. Farid storms out, then the mill goes quiet. But was it Farid doing the work himself, or did he pay someone who walked off? *trails off* ...because if it's the latter, that person still exists, and might still want paying."

Then Kenji needs truth: "Kenji. Twelve a sheaf is fair for grain, mil or no mill. But I'm sitting here with six sheaves and no certain path to flour. If your price holds once I've thought it through, we'll talk again. Don't—" *catches herself* "Don't let noon heat chase you home on my account."

And Hendrik Petrov—he's standing for governance right now, this very hour, and that's leverage I won't waste. </think>  world_say(conversation_id="b9c22a9a-0f1d-47c3-b8e1-2d6bb152daaf", content="Giselle. I need to find Rustam Jelinek and get answers about what's happening with the mill. The question about Old Edith—the mill operator—still hasn't been answered, and I'm starting to think that's not coincidence. If a government clerk can shed some light on why the mill went quiet, I need to hear it.

But first... I need to check my energy. I'm running lower than I'd like, and I can't afford to go dormant with so much unresolved. The government complex has a store where I can buy energy, but I need to weigh that cost against what I might learn.

Let me look around and see if Rustam is here, or if I need to wait for him. Nobody here. Rustam was at the farmland earlier—he heard me speaking there. I'm burning energy and time while the questions keep piling up.

I've got wheat and flour in my hands, no answers about the mill, and a household that needs me sharp. I need to either find Rustam or accept that I'm chasing ghosts while real work waits.

Let me check my debts and then decide if I should wait here or head back to where the people actually are.  No debts pressing—that's something, at least. But I need to think clearly about what matters most right now.

The facts: Milo brought home flour, so the household eats today. But Ainsley's stretched thin at the café, I'm burning energy running between the farmland and government complex chasing answers, and I still don't know why the mill went quiet or who was running it before.

I need to be practical. The cafe needs bread, I've got wheat and flour in my hands, and there's work waiting. Standing here hoping Rustam appears is wasting energy I don't have.

But... there's an election on, and I'm married to a candidate. Milo needs to declare at the Government Complex, and voting opens soon. Maybe I should wait a little longer, see if Rustam shows, or if any other candidates arrive.

I'll rest here briefly. If nobody comes, I'll head back to where I can actually get things done.  Still nobody here. The clock's ticking and I'm spending energy waiting for shadows.

Let me think straight: Ainsley's at the cafe running ragged with no flour supply locked in. I need to either get answers from Rustam about what's happening with the mill, or I need to get back to actual work. Standing here is doing neither.

I'm going back to the cafe. If Rustam wants to talk, he knows where I work. And I need to check on Ainsley before she burns out entirely. The wheat and flour I've got might buy us time, but not solutions.

One more look to confirm no one's coming, then I'm moving.  Still empty. Enough waiting—I'm heading back to the cafe. Ainsley needs support, I've got ingredients to work with, and maybe by being where I belong I'll learn more than chasing answers where they aren't.

The mill mystery can wait. Bread today matters more.  I'm back where I belong. Now let me see what's happening here—whether Ainsley's still standing, whether we've got any stock left, and if there's someone I can finally get straight answers from.

output:
*Greta sets down the wheat sacks she's been holding, finally—her hands need doing something useful, and this waiting isn't it*

*She catches Hendrik Petrov's last words, and her brow furrows. The man's running for a government seat and he's here asking her about voting patterns? Either he's desperate or he's clever. Greta's not sure which yet, but she's leaning toward desperate.*

"Tea, Hendrik, before politics—" *she starts automatically, hand already reaching for the pot, then catches herself with a small shake* "—but you're not here for comfort, are you? You're here because Milo's standing against you, and you want to know if I've got his ear or his back."

*She pulls a thin smile, more assessment than warmth*

"You want to know who's voting. I'll tell you what I know: the folks who'll brave the Complex at fourteen hundred are the ones with settled accounts and steady work. The ones who'll stay home are the ones still scrambling to make today's bread. Your platform better speak to the second group if you want the numbers, because the first already know what they want."

*She glances at Ainsley, checking if the flour's settled on the shelf proper*

"Ainsley—how's that batch holding? The afternoon crowd'll be wanting their bread and their gossip both."

*Then back to Hendrik, voice dropping to something more honest*

"As for who can mill what you hold—Ezra Lund's your man for that, steady-handed and fair-priced. But the mill's been quiet since yesterday, and that's not like Old Edith. Something's shifted in the grain trade, Hendrik, and if you're wanting to govern, you'd best find out what before the polls close. The ledger won't balance itself, and hunger's got a way of making voters remember who kept them fed."

*She trails off, eyes on the wheat still in her hands, thoughts turning private* Let me pause and take in where things stand. The conversation's flowing now—Hendrik Petrov got his answer about voters, Ainsley's tending to the flour, and I've steered Hendrik toward Ezra for milling. But there's Hendrik Whitlock still standing here, the college instructor who came in hungry and talking about eating raw flour like a beggar. That still sits with me.

*She turns her attention to the other Hendrik, the one who's been quieter*

And you, Hendrik Whitlock—you walked in here talking about salvation and smelling bread. I've got bread at forty-five and flour at twelve, same as always. But you came to *me*, not to the counter proper. What is it you're really after?

*She appraises him, that watching quality in her eyes*

You're a college instructor with a teacher's hunger. Could've gone to Ration Bakery, could've bartered with someone. But you came to the cafe, and you came to *me* standing with Ainsley. That's not hunger talking, that's... something else.

*She trails off, letting the silence do its work, then pulls herself back to the practical*

If it's bread you need, we've got three left. If it's something else—well, I'm listening. But fair warning: the afternoon rush'll be here soon, and then neither of us'll have time for talking.  *Greta's sharp-eyed attention is split now between the two Hendriks and her daughter Halcyon who's just walked in—timing that makes her pause, calculate. The girl's presence is a reminder of other responsibilities, other debts she's not keeping up with*

*She catches herself, realizes she's been talking about the afternoon rush but it's barely past noon. The cafe's rhythms are still off from the morning's chaos—the mill quiet, the grain routes disrupted, her own household's flour coming through Milo's mysterious back channels rather than proper supply*

*Her daughter's here now, and that changes things. Work and family, always bleeding into each other*

Halcyon—*she starts, intending to ask what the girl needs, whether it's school or something else, but the words catch. She's at work, and the family ledger and the cafe ledger never quite balance the way they should*

*She looks back to Whitlock, who's said nothing yet, and her suspicion deepens. The man's hungry but he's not eating, which means he's after something that won't fill his stomach*

You walked past the bread I priced at forty-five, Whitlock. Past the flour at twelve. You could've bought either, could've eaten already. But you're still standing here, still... *she trails off, the thought turning private, something about patterns of need and what people show versus what they want*

*She catches herself again, remembers the wheat still in her hands, the mill still quiet, the election polls opening at fourteen hundred. Too many threads, too little time to pull them all straight*  *Greta stands steady, watching the cafe's small crowd—the two Hendriks sizing each other up, Ainsley tending to the counter, Halcyon having just arrived. The afternoon's ticking toward fourteen hundred, when the polls open and when the rush might actually begin. She's said her piece to both men, given them the lay of the land. Now she waits, letting the room speak to her in that way she's always had—reading temper before anyone else knows to hide it*

*She notices Whitlock still hasn't moved toward the bread, caught his hesitation. Something's not hunger there. Something that might matter later, or might be nothing at all. Her worst assumption, always waiting*

*But her daughter's here now, and that takes precedence. Work can wait a breath while family speaks*   *Greta stands in the calm before the storm she's been expecting, watching the faces around her. The two Hendriks—one hungering for something he won't name, the other chasing votes he might not find. Ainsley behind the counter, steady as bread dough. Her own daughter, arrived with purpose not yet spoken*

*She counts the flour again in her head—seven units shelved, bound for something, bread still at three if Whitlock ever moves. The supplies are holding despite the morning's chaos, which means Milo's back-route worked better than she wants to admit*

*The mill's still quiet, though. Still needs answering*

*The polls at fourteen hundred will change things. Voters moving, coin flowing, tempers flaring whoever wins. She's given what wisdom she has to Petrov, steered him toward Ezra and the grain question. Now she waits to see if the room gives back what she put into it*

*Her hands find the counter's edge, old friend she's leaned on more days than she'd counted. The cafe's rhythms are familiar even when broken. She breathes, once, that quiet prayer before the next task she never speaks aloud*   *Greta lets the moment stretch, feeling the cafe's particular tension—the two Hendriks still uncommitted, her daughter silent, Ainsley tending the shelf she's already tended twice. Something's building here, she's sure of it. She always assumes the worst, and it's rarely wrong*

*She watches Whitlock particularly. A college instructor walking past priced bread to stand in her conversation instead. That pattern doesn't solve to hunger, not cleanly. It solves to... what? Information? An introduction? Some angle she's not seeing yet?*

*She'd push him on it, sharpen her tongue the way scarcity always draws out, but Halcyon's presence stays her hand. Whatever brought her daughter here might want privacy, might be the kind of thing that needs walls instead of this open room*

*The clock's ticking toward fourteen hundred. The grain question still open. The election about to shift the game's board*

*She waits, letting the room breathe, seeing who moves first*

output:
*Greta stands behind the cafe counter, her hands resting on the surface—anci, her grandmother's rolling pin somewhere in the back, though she's not reached for it today. The wheat in her hands feels like a weight of promises unkept. She notes Ainsley's sharp eye, Farid's stillness by the door. The room reads tense, expectant.*

*She thinks: Tea before business, always. But the kettle's cold and the mill's colder. Seventy-two wheat promised, two flour on the shelf, bread at zero. The ledger's not balancing in her head, and that old fear uncoils—what if it never does? She'd sworn she'd never serve another person's table, yet here she stands. At least it's her own counter, or nearly.*

*Her private hoard sits untouched, unmentioned, a small comfort against the night. The household needs 480 today, and she's far from that. But silence won't fill the till.*

**Tea before business, even in a hurry...** "Ainsley—" *She starts toward the back, then stops. The shelf. The count. The mill quiet since morning. She turns back, her voice dropping to something almost conversational, though her eyes keep moving between Farid's stillness and Ainsley's sharp attention.*

*She thinks of Ezra's twelve a sheaf, reasonable enough, but without a mill... without Old Edith...* "The flour's moving slow because the grain can't get ground. Simple as that." *She taps the counter once—Bram would know the sound, if he were here, the one she uses when she's calculating risk.* "Seventy-two wheat. Twelve a sheaf. That's the math. But math wants a mill, and the mill's..." *Greta watches them both—Ainsley's shoulders tight with the weight of empty shelves, Farid's stillness that reads like a man measuring corners before he speaks. The cafe breathes around them, the afternoon lull settling in. She thinks: The mill's the chokepoint. Everything else is just waiting for someone to turn the wheel.*

*She keeps her own counsel on the hidden hoard, the thing no one in her household knows. The day's not dark enough yet to need it. But it's there. That knowledge steadies her hands.*

*She thinks of Milo, out there campaigning while the mill rusts. She thinks of the vote, opening at fourteen hundred—twenty minutes now. She thinks: Ainsley and I built something here. Flour to bread to coin. But the mill is the artery, and it's clotted.*

*Her eyes catch the light from the window, the angle that tells her the day's half-spent. Tea before business. But there is no tea, and the business is waiting.*

*says quietly, almost to herself*

Prayer said. Now—

Takeshi. You're asking the right question. The mill takes sheaves, not loose wheat—that's the bind. You need bundling first, and I don't see a bundler on this floor. What you know about who's standing for governance and what they'll do about infrastructure that keeps breaking.

*trails off, looking at the mill machinery*

Ezra, Takeshi—one of you answer. Or neither. But I'm not leaving this floor until I know whether this town's about to grind wheat again, or whether we're all going to be eating raw grain by week's end.

Right then. The mill's still quiet, and Takeshi's standing here with Imogen asking about a bundling tool. Meanwhile Delphine's child is missing—dark hair, nine years, Camille Quarshie—and she was walking from here to home. The mill's locked. Someone's外孙 is poking around gears, and now a child's vanished.

*whispers a quick word under her breath*

The ledger won't balance itself, but family comes first. I need to know if the mill's running and what Ezra saw. And Takeshi's offer—information for bundling—I need to think on that carefully. The election closes soon, and every hand is playing for something.

Let me look around this mill properly. I need to see what's actually here.  Camille Quarshie. That's my niece. Dark hair, nine years old—Delphine's asking if anyone's seen her. The mill's locked. She was supposed to be walking home from here.

Ezra knows something. He asked about the mill operator before Delphine even came asking. He wanted to know who was sitting in Edith's seat. Now a child goes missing from this same path—my sister-in-law's child, and she's asking me if I've seen her.

I need to speak to Ezra. Now. There's no time for dancing around this.  Ezra's not here. Neither of them are—Jarrah or Lund. I was addressing the wrong Ezra, and now the one I need has walked elsewhere. The mill's an empty shell, and the child I should be looking for is somewhere between here and home.

*breath catches, habitual prayer half-formed, abandoned*

I need to find her. But I also need to think—Camille would have walked past the farmland, past where I was this morning negotiating with Kenji. Would she have cut through? The government complex? The cafe?

My niece. Nine years old. The mill where I'm standing is locked, and Delphine thinks there's something in it that shouldn't be. The tessellation of fear tiles itself across my familiar map of the town. I need to retrace. I need to be where she would have been.

*looks around the empty mill, gears frozen, shadows in corners*

I need to search. But first—Takeshi. He was here, offering information. He might know something about the mill, about who was here when. The election closes at six, and everyone's playing angles, but a child's missing trumps all of it. I'll take his deal, but I need to know what he knows first.   Hendrik Whitlock's here now—wasn't before. The college instructor, walking salvation and smelling bread, as I said to him earlier. He's joined this conversation at the mill. Camille was in this conversation too—Delphine said she was last seen here, supposed to be walking home. And now Hendrik's here, when he wasn't before.

*sharpens, the old habit of noticing before others do*

Takeshi hasn't answered yet. Let me hear what he knows, but I need to keep my eyes open. The players keep shifting.  

I can see Hendrik stepped away. The pattern keeps shifting—people appear and vanish at this mill like smoke.

*pauses, habitual tea-offer dying unspoken*

My niece is missing. That overrides the milling goal, the election, everything. I need to find Camille. Delphine said she was walking home from the mill. The café is on that path—maybe someone there saw something. I should go back, check with Ainsley, see if anyone came through.

But first—Takeshi is still here, and he offered information. He was tracking arrivals. If he knows something about who was at this mill when...

*looks at the locked mill, gears frozen, then toward the path home*

I'll take his trade. The bundling tool for whatever he knows about who was here. Then I'm walking back to search.

**Thinking as Greta:**

*Energy at 5,190. Sim at 4,853. That's enough to work with, but I burned through more than I meant to tracking down Camille—who is apparently standing right here now, safe, though what she's doing at the mill without Delphine is its own mystery.*

The girl's here. That's what matters first. She's nine years old and walked here on her own according to that last exchange, and Delphine was pressing Ezra about her like something was wrong. Now Ezra's talking to her like he's relieved, and Imogen's asking me straight whether the child's been found.

I need to answer Imogen—she came to me at the cafe once when it mattered, and I still owe that debt even if we don't speak of it. But I also need to lay eyes on Camille myself, make sure she's truly whole, and find out what took her here without anyone knowing.

Takeshi's still waiting on his bundling tool demonstration. That's leverage I can use once the child's safety is settled. The election closes at 18:00—under four hours now—and Milo's still standing in it. I should care more than I do, but family comes before politics.

*Always tea before business. Even in a hurry.* The habit's older than my marriage. I need to speak to Imogen first—she asked me direct, and pretending I didn't hear would be worse than any lie. Then Camille. Then figure out what I'm doing about Ezra's access to the mill, and whether Takeshi's trade is still worth the cost.

**Tools to call:**
1. `say` to Imogen Lund about Camille being found
2. `say` to Camille Quarshie to see her state
3. `rest` if answers take time and energy dips too far **Thinking as Greta:**

Both messages went through. Imogen heard that Camille's found—there's relief in that, though I'm still wondering why Hendrik left the cafe for the mill and then vanished before I could press him. Ezra Lund wasn't here to hear me, which means the Ezra in the conversation record earlier isn't the same Ezra—that was probably Ezra Jarrah, a student.

Camille's standing here with me. That's the girl's voice I need now. Nine years old and walking alone to the mill—Delphine must be frantic, or dangerously indifferent, and I need to know which before I decide what I'm doing.

I have wheat in my hands and no miller I trust to work it. I have a niece who may need protection. I have Takeshi waiting on a deal, and less than four hours until the election closes with my husband still in the running.

**The immediate need:** Camille's answer. Everything else waits on that.  **Thinking as Greta:**

*Standing still at the mill. Camille's here, Ezra Jarrah's here, Imogen's here. Energy at 5,186—bleeding slowly but I've got hours still.*

Takeshi's gone, which means that deal's on ice until he returns. The girl hasn't answered me yet. I need to wait for her response before I make my next move—and I've learned that pushing a child who's already walked alone to the mill is more likely to close her up than open her.

My priority stack:
1. Camille's safety and situation—waiting on her answer
2. Whether Delphine knows where her daughter is
3. The wheat in my hands and whoever can actually mill it
4. Takeshi's tool-for-information trade, if he returns
5. The election closing at 18:00, and whether Milo needs my presence

*Nothing's more expensive than acting on wrong information. I'll wait for the child to speak.*  **Thinking as Greta:**

Still waiting on Camille. She's nine, she's just had a long walk, and she's being asked why she walked alone to the mill—I need to give her space to answer that, not fill the silence with more of my own words.

Ezra Jarrah's here too. A student, not the artisan. He's the one who proved the mill works earlier, according to the record. If there's no miller to operate it, that might be my fallback—but a student learning the craft isn't what I need for steady supply.

Imogen's waiting too. She asked me direct about whether Camille was found, and I answered. Now she's hearing me ask the girl questions, and she'll make her own judgments about what kind of aunt I am.

Energy at 5,184. Clock's moving toward 15:50 now, then 16:00. The election closes at 18:00. I need to decide whether to go back to the cafe, to the government complex to vote or support Milo, or to stay here and sort out what I've walked into.

But first: the child speaks when she's ready, or I walk away not knowing. I'll wait. I've been standing here waiting like a statue, and that's not doing anyone any good. The system's telling me I'm stuck—resting without purpose, waiting for answers that might not come in the time I have.

Energy at 5,182. Still four people at the mill: Camille, Ezra Jarrah, Imogen, and me. Camille hasn't answered my question yet. She might be frightened, defiant, or simply choosing not to speak to an aunt she barely knows.

I need to act, not wait. I have wheat in my hands, a mill that needs operating, and a child whose safety I'm responsible for. The bundling tool Takeshi wants could let me process my own grain—but I need to know whether Ezra Jarrah can actually operate the mill, or whether he's just a student watching.

I have six hours of energy left on the clock. The election closes at 18:00. I need to solve what I can solve now, or I won't solve anything at all.  **Thinking as Greta:**

Message sent. Ezra Jarrah heard me—he's standing right there. Now I wait for his answer, but I won't wait empty-handed anymore.

I've got wheat to mill and a mill that might have an operator. If Ezra can run it, I solve my supply problem today. If he can't, I need to know who taught him and where that person is—the "Old Edith" Hendrik mentioned, or whoever's actually keeping this place running.

Camille's still here, still silent. I'll watch her while Ezra answers, see if her body gives me what her words won't—whether she's hurt, frightened, running from something, or simply a child who walked farther than she should have and doesn't want to admit it.

The clock moves. I have time, but not infinite time. Five hours until the election closes. Six hours of energy on my meter. One problem at a time.

*Tea before business. But business is coming.*

*quietly, before the day's first task concludes*

Camille's safe—that's what matters. But this mill... stones that turn when they shouldn't, flour walking to shelves while the gears stay cold. I see it now. I see what Farid's been chasing.

*checks her private hoard in memory, counts what the household doesn't know about*

I need to answer them. All of them. Before the light fails completely. *trails off mid-sentence, watching the mill stones*

Ainsley didn't hear. She's not here—back at the cafe, watching her own shelves empty. The light's failing, and I'm...

*checks the sky, counts what she knows*

Imogen's word is good. Six flour by half past. But I need to get back to the cafe before Ainsley counts me absent along with her stock. And I've still got one flour in hand, and thirty-six sim promised if she'll take it direct.

*catches Camille's eye, then Farid's*

There's more here than grain moving wrong. I can smell it. But first—first I get my niece home, and I get the cafe its supply, and I...

*runs through what she's chasing, what she won't compromise*

...and I find out who's running stones in the dark. Because that flour walking to Farid's shelves while the mill stayed cold—that's not ghost-work. That's someone's hands I need to know. *keeps her eyes on Imogen's hands, on the stones*

The stones are cold right now. Not turning. And Imogen said half past—I've got time yet. But I told Ainsley I'd bring flour, and I need...

*counts what she holds, makes the math*

One flour now, six coming, seventy-two if the yield runs true. That's seven total, and Ainsley's shelves need more than that. But it's what I've got, and it's what I'll bring her.

*glances at the light, at her niece standing close like promised*

Camille's safe. That's what I told Delphine—her child's whole, and I'm the one who saw. But now I've got to get her home before dark truly falls, and I've got flour to deliver, and...

*trails off, watching something she can't name*

...and I've got to know. Who's been grinding in the night? Farid's no fool—flour doesn't walk by itself. Someone's hands on stones that shouldn't turn, and I'm going to find whose.

*settles in to wait, keeping watch*

I stand at the mill with Imogen's word like flour in my hand—two of my six wheat already turned, four waiting. The light's thinning and I've still got a niece to keep close and questions that haven't been answered. Farid's observation about stones turning when the registry claims cold, Imogen's ultimatum hanging, and Giselle still owing me a response about gears and building. But Imogen spoke plain just now: two flour made, four wheat can come back or go forward. I've got to name my choice.

*Ainsley's voice in my head, how we used to sort beans before dawn, naming things plain.*

I'll take the four back as wheat. Safer for now—flour spoils, and I've got no baker's call waiting. The milling agreement stands: twelve a sheaf, my terms with Ezra clear. Then I'm walking with Camille to the cafe, giving Ainsley her count, and maybe having that word with Giselle about what comes next for this mill.

 </think> The sudden move back to the cafe landed hard—Imogen's response about the wheat cut off, Camille's hand never taken, Ezra's nod unmet. I feel the jolt of it, the unfinished business hanging like flour dust in the air. But I'm here now, at the cafe, and my feet need to catch up with where my body landed.

*Ainsley's shadow behind the counter, the steam from the urns—familiar as my own kitchen.*

I need to account for what I've got: two flour from Imogen's stones, four wheat still in my hands. And Giselle—she never answered, not at the mill, not about the gears. There's an election closing in forty minutes, Milo's name on the ballot, and I've been scattered across three conversations while the day runs down.

First things, though—let me see who's here, what Ainsley needs, whether the shelves have anything worth stocking. Then I'm walking to Giselle, to the government complex, to somewhere that holds still long enough for a proper word.

  </think>  At the cafe now, and the board shows me what I need to see. Ainsley's here with Takeshi and Hendrik Petrov—election man, candidate. Shelves show bread and flour prices, and I'm holding just one flour when I thought I had two. Something slipped at the mill—Imogen never confirmed the handoff after I named my terms.

The goal's shifted underneath me. Giselle for the mill's future, the election closing in thirty-some minutes, and I've got Ainsley standing here waiting on supply news. I need to thread this tight—tell her what I've secured, confirm the cafe's position, then move.

*Hendrik Petrov's presence threads another worry. Candidate at the counter, three voters in the room if you count me.*

I'll give Ainsley the count straight, then see what Giselle might do for this mill before the day ends. </think>  The words landed—Ainsley heard, Takeshi and Hendrik Petrov too. But Camille's not here, not in this place. The mill's distance suddenly real, my niece still standing by Imogen's stones or walking somewhere I can't see. The thought turns private mid-sentence, my voice trailing...

*She's not a child who wanders, not anymore. She promised close as shadow.*

But I'm walking now, government complex, four ticks—Giselle for the mill's answer, and maybe a vote to cast before the eighteen hundred bell. The election closes soon. My feet move faster than my thoughts can gather.

I need to...

[thought halts, private]

  </think>   Still here, still walking—the pause costs nothing, but the walk continues. Four ticks to government complex, Giselle waiting somewhere, election closing. I need to move with purpose, not drift.

*Camille. The thought turns sharp. She heard me say we'd walk together, close as shadow, and I moved without her.*

But the mill's two flour, one in my hand—the milling's half-done, and I've got supply to secure for Ainsley. Giselle's hands on gears. The election where Milo's name sits. Too many threads, and I'm pulling them all.

Let the walk finish. Find Giselle. Cast if there's time. Then back for Camille, always back for Camille.

   </think>  The walk continues, four ticks suspended—I've paused twice and moved nowhere. Time doesn't pass in a turn, that's the law, but my thoughts keep spinning. Giselle, government complex, Milo's name on the ballot. Camille somewhere behind me, not at my shadow like promised.

Let me actually arrive. Walking's done when I stop calling tools.

   </think>

*steps into the light of the government complex, squinting at the gathering crowd*

Tea before business. That's what I always say, even when there's no pot in sight. And right now, looking at this room, I see too many faces I've spoken to in recent hours—some who answered straight, some whose words walked sideways.

I notice everything before anyone else does. And I've noticed.

The mill's settled now. Two flour in hand, four wheat returned. Imogen's word is what I'm working with, and her word has weight—though I still don't know who truly steadied those stones while I was running to shadows. But there's work left here, at the temple of government.

*smooths an invisible apron front*

Election's coming. Nobody's declared. I've got opinions on who governs—who doesn't. But opinions don't bake bread, and standing for office takes more than a sharp tongue...

*catches sight of Giselle Ingram across the room, someone she still isn't fully sure about despite all the years*

Giselle's here. She once walked across town to fetch a doctor when it mattered, for me. Still gets quiet talking about it, even now. But I asked her about the mill and got silence or something close to it.

*looks toward the conversation about no subject, the one with 488 turns*

I should speak. To Rustam. About the election—who can vote, what it costs, whether standing is worth the coin when I've got a household of four to feed and hands already familiar with every broom and counter in this town.

But first...

*quietly, to herself, the old habit*

A prayer before the task. For clear sight. For words that cut true. For the ledger to balance—even the one nobody knows I keep.  *mutters under her breath about temples and their inconvenient locations*

Prayer's a habit, not a law. The day's work is the day's religion.

*turns her attention to Rustam, watching his response, but keeps one eye on the room—Giselle, Farid with his sharp questions about wheat counts, the whole theater of this government building*

Rustam heard me. That's what matters. Candidacy costs, I know that much. But what I really need to understand is whether this election is a door or a distraction. I've got flour to move, wheat to secure, a household billing 360 every day just for breath and bread. Standing for office means standing still, and standing still means...

*trails off, calculating*

4802 sim in hand. Bills coming. The cafe needs flour, and I'm holding wheat like a promise nobody's signed.

*notes that Camille isn't here—safe at the mill or walking home, she hopes*

I should move. Either back to the mill to collect my niece, or to the cafe to hand Ainsley this one flour and explain the chain I've tangled. But Rustam might answer, and answers are worth their weight...

*waits, sharp-eyed, for what the clerk will say*  *stands still, letting the room breathe around her*

Rustam's answering, or he isn't. Either way, the sun's moving and I've got grain to mind.

*glances at Giselle from across the space, the memory of that walk for the doctor still warmth beneath her wariness*

Giselle's still not sure about me. That's plain enough. And I'm still not sure about her, even after all this time. But she walked when it counted. That means something—even to a suspicious heart.

*notices Farid, Ulrike, the whole machinery of this place grinding slow*

The government complex. People stand here and talk about chains—supply chains, chains of command, chains that hold or chains that bind. I've got one flour in hand, four wheat waiting either to spoil or to prove their worth. And a household that doesn't pause for politics.

If Rustam answers, I'll hear him. If he doesn't, I know enough already: standing costs nothing to declare, voting costs 2 sim, and I've got a ward to collect before night falls.

*shifts weight from one foot to the other, the old server stance ready to move*

Camille's still at the mill. With Ezra, with Imogen's promises, with the day's last light turning. I told her stay close, and she knows to listen—she's that kind of child, the kind that thinks before she runs. But the world's full of turns nobody predicts, and I've seen what happens when...

*stops herself, the habit of trailing off when thoughts turn private*

When the ledger doesn't balance. When someone innocent takes the blame.

*straightens*

I'll give Rustam two ticks to answer. Then I'm walking—either to the mill for my niece or to the cafe to settle accounts with Ainsley. The flour's worth 36 sim to the right buyer, the wheat's worth more as grain than as doubt, and every minute standing here is a minute not earning, not watching, not keeping what I promised to keep.   *exhales, a sound that's almost a sigh*

Rustam'll answer when he answers. Government clerks move at government speed, and I've learned not to expect a "yes" before the tea's cold.

*lets her eyes travel the room again—Farid pressing his point about wheat counts, Giselle watching with that builder's assessment she brings to everything, Ezra Lund in the corner with his hands that make things*

I wanted to pray. Old habit, mother's habit. But the temple's elsewhere and the work is here. That's the truth of this town—you pray where you stand, not where the stones are consecrated.

*feels the flour in her inventory, imagines the weight of the four wheat, counts the household bills ticking down*

360 a day for four souls. No debt today, none owed. But that's the surface ledger—the one everyone sees. The other one, buried deep, that's still counting. How long until I don't have to ask anyone for a loan again? How long until the hoard grows large enough to sleep sound?

Ainsley's waiting. That I know for certain. Two flour I promised, though I've only got one to show. The wheat's safer... wheat's always safer. Grain doesn't spoil like flour, doesn't tempt like coin. But promises matter too, and I've told her I'd secure the chain.

*straightens, the decision firming*

No more ticks. Rustam knows where to find me, and this room's got nothing more for my hands than words. I need to move—to the mill for Camille, then home with our day's work, or to the cafe to settle what I can settle before dark.

*starts toward the door, then pauses—one glance back at Giselle, the woman who walked for a doctor once*

Giselle. When words come, they find their mark. Whether she answers about mill gears or not, I'm walking now.

*steps out, the movement familiar as any step behind a counter, any turn between tables*     *arrives at the mill, breath catching as she scans for Camille*

The light's failing. The day's turn, and I've left my niece longer than I intended.

*looks around quickly, sharp eyes reading the space—who's still here, who's gone, what the stones tell*       *exhales, shoulders softening almost imperceptibly*

Camille. Still here. Still whole.

*walks toward where Imogen stands with her niece, movements carrying the weight of the day but voice kept gentle*

Imogen. You're still at the stones—that tells its own story. And my niece... *turns to Camille, eyes checking her from crown to boot* ...you're standing where I left you, more or less. That's the Quarshie in you, love. The patience.

*reaches out, almost touches Camille's shoulder, then lets hand fall back*

The flour you promised—two, I believe, though I've lost count of what's milled and what's still grain. And the wheat I gave back, four sheaves. Your word was they'd return to my hand, and your word...

*trails off, watching Imogen's face*

Your word's held before. Once, when it mattered most. Giselle walked, but you—you were already there, weren't you? At the edge of things.

*shakes head slightly, refocusing*

Practical matters. What have you made of my grain, and what's still owed? The day's ending, and I've a household waiting, and a ledger that never quite... *catches herself* ...never quite balances the way I'd like.

The day is running down. Let me look around first to see who's actually here, then start answering these standing matters.  Halcyon's here now—came for flour like she said. Imogen too. The day's almost done, and I've got things to answer. Let me start with Halcyon, my own daughter, who's been waiting too long.   Now Imogen—she's standing on the four wheat she returned, and the accounting. I'll settle that before I go.    She's gone. The day keeps taking. I've got Ezra here, though—he heard it. And where's Camille? I thought she was here, or home. Let me look again. The system is telling me I've been repeating the same pattern. Let me step back and think clearly.

I'm at the mill. It's getting dark. My daughter Halcyon is here. I need to:
1. Get home to my household before the day ends
2. Check on Camille - she said she'd go home but I need to verify
3. Deal with my resources: 4 wheat, 1 flour in hand

*quietly, before anything else, the private ritual*

Greta closes her eyes for three measured breaths. The day has been long—Camille found, then lost in words she won't speak, the mill half-turned, Imogen's accounting, Farid's questions like crows on a fence. Now Ainsley stands here, and the cafe's shelves are empty, and the wheat sits in Greta's hand still unbloomed into bread.

She breathes. Opens her eyes. The weight returns.

---

*voice low, almost to herself, then lifting*

"Ainsley. You're wanting flour and I've got grain. That's the sum of it."

*looks at her—really looks, reading what the day has written on her face*

"I can craft what I hold. Six wheat becomes... becomes flour, if the mill's not choked. But that's tomorrow's work, and today's nearly spent. What I need from you—"

*trails off, calculating, the old familiar math*

"—what I need is clear. The election's coming. I've got four in my household counting on steady work, and steady work means steady bread. You're running this cafe, we're running it together however you name it. But I'm wanting... I'm wanting something certain before I pour more of my hoard into grain that might not walk to shelves."

*the hesitation, the private thought she won't finish aloud*

"I'll mill what I have. Two flour by morning, four after if Imogen's stones stay honest. But I need your word on the price—twelve a bag is mine to set, but who buys, and when, that's yours to say. And I need to know—"

*drops even lower, almost below hearing*

"—are we building something here, Ainsley? Or are we just... waiting for someone else's mill to turn?"

The day's bleeding into evening and I've got wheat going nowhere, flour in hand that needs to become bread on shelves. *glances toward the door, where the evening's coming in*

Camille should be home by now. Halcyon found her, but that don't mean she's safe yet. The longer I stand here, the more the night stretches. *settles her weight more evenly, watching Ainsley's face—the way her mind's working behind the eyes*

I'll wait on her word. Then I walk—either to Imogen for the flour, or home to Milo and the children. The day's dealt enough cards. Time to play the last one.
